chapter: Maynard Ferguson and the drinking life
title: Surviving the lifestyle
summary: At nearly 70, he is in good health, runs, and cannot explain why others did not make it.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Gin mills. Oh yeah, I mean that’s when you should drink is when you play. We used to have the booze — I went to Eddie Condon’s club. I mean I played there for three years after that, I was the house drummer there. But I don’t know how far you want to get into this. You probably want to get into the Woody Herman years.
I mean you look pretty good.
Pretty good is not quite good. I’m going to be 70 on my next birthday and I ran up a hill yesterday. I run. And they can’t find anything wrong with me.
But a lot of guys didn’t make it.

Well I don’t know why. I mean my grandfather lived to be 100. But see I quit smoking cigarettes, I mean so I don’t have that. I mean somebody said once that “a cat wouldn’t even eat your liver.” Well every time I go over to the VA, which I’m going to go tomorrow morning, they can’t find anything — they say, “there’s nothing wrong with you.” I’ve got the results from my bloodwork. It said, “you’re Vitamin D deficient.” I guess that’s the new big thing. But now — because in the wintertime the sun — I sit out in the sun, I mean I can’t even get a sunburn. I don’t know if it’s because of my pigmentation or whatever.
